blockMcqs.question: What distinguishes concurrency from parallelism?
options: Concurrency needs more cores; parallelism needs one
They are two names for the same thing
Concurrency is structure; parallelism is simultaneous execution
Parallelism only applies to I/O work
blockMcqs.explanation: You can interleave tasks on one core, but running at the same instant needs many cores.

blockMcqs.question: Why is `count = count + 1` not thread-safe?
options: It allocates memory on every call
Reads are slower than writes
It is a read-modify-write that can interleave
The compiler refuses to optimize it
blockMcqs.explanation: Two threads can both read the old value and both write the same result, losing one update.

blockMcqs.question: What is the most common way to prevent deadlock?
options: Use only a single global lock everywhere
Acquire locks in a fixed global order
Never release a lock once acquired
Allow any thread to preempt any other
blockMcqs.explanation: A consistent ordering removes circular wait, one of the four required conditions.

blockMcqs.question: What does compare-and-swap do?
options: Locks memory until the writer finishes
Sorts two values into ascending order
Sets memory to new only if it equals expected
Copies one variable's value into another
blockMcqs.explanation: The atomic conditional write underpins lock-free retry loops on a single variable.

blockMcqs.question: Why might thread B never see a value thread A wrote?
options: Threads cannot share any memory
The variable was declared too small
No happens-before edge forces visibility
B started running before A was created
blockMcqs.explanation: Store buffers and reordering hide writes unless a lock, atomic, or barrier links the two.

blockMcqs.question: What is the event loop's main weakness?
options: It cannot handle network I/O at all
It requires locks for every callback
A CPU-heavy callback blocks all other work
It needs one thread per connection
blockMcqs.explanation: A single thread can't span cores, so any long computation starves every pending callback.

blockMcqs.question: Why is Redis effectively race-free on its data?
options: It locks every key before access
It copies data between threads
One thread runs each command atomically
It forbids concurrent connections
blockMcqs.explanation: A single-threaded event loop means commands never interleave, so no locks are needed.

blockMcqs.question: What does Java's `volatile` guarantee for `count++`?
options: Full atomicity of the increment
Visibility and ordering, but not atomicity
A lock around the operation
Protection from spurious wakeups
blockMcqs.explanation: The read-modify-write still races; only an atomic type or lock makes it safe.
